title: Cycles and Caches
focus: Constant-space tricks, the design question they actually ask, and the two-string DP that anchors the whole lane.

cards.title: Fast and Slow on an Array
cards.trigger: Values are in range 1..n and you must find a duplicate or a missing number in O(1) space.
cards.recall: Write the duplicate finder from memory. Then answer the part that makes it click: what makes `i -> nums[i]` a linked list, and why does a duplicate value guarantee a cycle?
useWhen: Find the duplicate without modifying the array and without extra space
Find all missing or all duplicate numbers in 1..n
First missing positive
Set mismatch, one duplicated and one missing
Any 'values are a permutation of 1..n' phrasing
template: # Treat i -> nums[i] as a linked list. Duplicates create a cycle.
slow = nums[0]                 # phase 2: find the entry point
# Cyclic sort: put every value at its own index, then scan
if 0 <= j < n and nums[i] != nums[j]:
nums[i], nums[j] = nums[j], nums[i]   # swap, do NOT advance
# now any index where nums[i] != i+1 is missing or duplicated
keyInsights: The cyclic sort swap does not advance `i`, because the value you just swapped in also needs placing. Advancing is the classic bug
Floyd here needs read-only input. If mutation is allowed, negative-marking is simpler and just as fast
The two-phase structure is identical to linked-list cycle entry. Recognise them as one technique
cards.trap: 'Do it without modifying the array AND in O(1) space AND explain why it terminates.' The termination argument is pigeonhole: n+1 values in n slots forces a repeat.

cards.title: LRU Cache
cards.trigger: O(1) get and put with eviction by recency. This is the most-asked design question in the set.
cards.recall: Sketch the structure from memory: what does the map store, and what do the two sentinels remove from the code? Then write `_remove` and `_insert_front`.
useWhen: LRU or LFU eviction
Browser history and back-forward navigation
Any O(1) 'most recent' or 'least recent' requirement
Ordered structures where you must delete from the middle in O(1)
Sliding window over unbounded keys
template: def __init__(self, k=0, v=0): self.k, self.v = k, v; self.prev = self.next = None
self.head, self.tail = Node(), Node()      # sentinels: no None checks ever
if k not in self.map: return -1
n = Node(k, v); self.map[k] = n; self._push_front(n)
self._remove(lru); del self.map[lru.k]     # need lru.k, hence storing k in the node
keyInsights: The node stores its own key so eviction can delete the map entry. Forgetting that leaks the map forever
Sentinels mean `_remove` never checks for None. That is worth four eliminated branches
`OrderedDict.move_to_end` solves it in five lines, but they want the linked list. Mention the shortcut, then build it
cards.trap: 'Now make it thread safe' or 'now make it LFU'. LFU needs frequency buckets, each an LRU list, plus a running minimum frequency. Know the shape.

cards.title: Serialize and Deserialize
cards.trigger: Convert a tree to a string and back, losslessly, for an arbitrary binary tree.
cards.recall: Write both directions from memory. Then answer the question underneath it: why do preorder plus null markers uniquely determine the tree, when preorder alone does not?
useWhen: Serialize and deserialize a binary tree or an n-ary tree
Encode and decode a list of strings, the same delimiter problem
Find duplicate subtrees, serialize each subtree as a key
Persist a tree to disk or send it over a wire
Subtree matching by string containment
template: it = iter(data.split(SEP))       # iterator carries the position for free
keyInsights: Null markers restore the shape. Preorder alone is ambiguous, which is why the classic rebuild needs inorder as well
An iterator is the cleanest cursor. Passing an index by value does not work in Python, and a list-of-one index is uglier
Serialised subtrees make excellent hash keys. That is the entire duplicate-subtrees problem
cards.trap: 'Values can be negative and multi-digit.' Your delimiter must be unambiguous. If you used a single character with no separator, this breaks you.

cards.title: Edit Distance
cards.trigger: Transform one string into another at minimum cost, or count how close they are.
cards.recall: Say what `dp[i][j]` means over the two prefixes, then write all three operations and their index offsets from memory. Getting which offset is insert versus delete is the whole exercise.
useWhen: Minimum edits to convert one string into another
One edit distance away, a linear special case
Delete operations to make two strings equal
Fuzzy matching and spell correction
Any two-string minimisation with unit costs
template: # dp[i][j] = min edits to turn a[:i] into b[:j]
for i in range(m + 1): dp[i][0] = i        # delete everything
for j in range(n + 1): dp[0][j] = j        # insert everything
keyInsights: Match is free and takes the diagonal. Every mismatch costs exactly one plus the best of three
The base rows are not decoration, they encode 'turn a prefix into the empty string', and they are what make the table correct
Drop the replace option and you get delete-only distance, which is m + n - 2 * LCS. Same table, different menu
cards.trap: 'Operations have different costs, replace costs 2.' The `1 +` becomes three separate costs. If you hardcoded the 1 you must restructure.

cards.title: Bipartite Check
cards.trigger: Split nodes into two groups such that every edge crosses between them.
cards.recall: Write the two-colour BFS from memory. Then answer: why must you loop over every node as a possible start, and what does an odd-length cycle have to do with any of this?
useWhen: Is this graph bipartite
Possible bipartition, dislikes between people
Two-team or two-machine assignment
Odd cycle detection in an undirected graph
Precondition check before bipartite matching
template: colour = [0] * n                # 0 unvisited, 1 and -1 the two sides
for start in range(n):          # graph may be disconnected
return False    # same colour across an edge
keyInsights: A graph is bipartite exactly when it has no odd-length cycle. That equivalence is the standard follow-up question
The outer loop over all starts is mandatory. A disconnected graph with one bad component still fails
Using 1 and -1 lets you write `-colour[u]` instead of a branch, which is small but reads well
cards.trap: 'Do it with union find instead.' Union each neighbour with the first neighbour, and fail if a node ends up unioned with its own neighbour. Being able to give both is a strong signal.
